review_text: Be sure to train before undertaking this trip—to the Base de las Torres and especially when doing the W, not to mention the O Circuits. However, it’s NOT the hardest hike in the park, as some reviewers claim. They apparently didn’t do the O Circuit with its brutal ascent to Gardner Pass and even more bone-crushing descent to Camp Gray (took me 10 exhausting hours, with the most gorgeous views of my life.) Also, ascending to Mirador Frances and further up to Britanico is at least as tough as hiking to the Torres. It’s not a walk in the park. Do your homework and listen to the locals. For the Torres, of course you need to be in shape, especially for the sections just below the lake, where you must climb large boulders on a steep incline. Going down may be even harder for those of us with busted knees. But the views are stunning, even in light rain. Go very early in the morning to avoid the damn crowds. Fortunately I set off from Camp Central at 5 am, and by 10 am I was roughly on the last third of the way back to Central, with droves of loud people clogging the trail. As is often the case, they disrespected the rules and trampled all over the landscape “because it was easier,” as one woman told me when I called her out to stay on the rocky trail. I enjoyed the light drizzle, some fog on the lake, and a beautiful rainbow. The people who went later did get to see the Torres in the sunshine, but I’m happy I had the woods to myself at the crack of dawn. People who stay at Camp Chileno have a definite advantage. The Mirador is only 1 1/2 hours away for them. But keep in mind that if you’re hiking from Frances the previous day, it’s a long day and the trail to Chileno is windy, steep, and slippery in places. Not fun with a heavy backpack. So I stayed in Central and hiked light, even though it’s a longer stretch, about 7 hours total at my age (59).

review_text: Yes, the water in the Marga Marga is sluggish and slow moving, but If the dam were not there, all that you would see a dry river bed. Because of the water management practices put in place, the estuary retains some of its water year-round and as a result, has helped the ecosystem. When you walk along the water, you can see a variety of bird life there. Up river outside of town, there is enough water to see lots of water plants, and on one memorable occasion, cows grazing on them knee-deep in the water. When I lived in Viña del Mar a few years ago, people who had grown up there remember when the Marga Marga had more water in it. But after years of drought and climate change, things have changed. It is a good thing that the water management system has been put in place.

review_text: Hello, with my family we took the 4 days and 3 nights tour to Salar de Uyuni. On Wednesday 05/04 at the border we were picked up by driver Jonatan I think surnamed Morales, excellent driver, very attentive, worried about how we were feeling about altitude sickness. We took an excellent photograph. A 7 as a person and driver. Already back to San Pedro de Atacama we traveled with Luis, the truth is that it is difficult to describe him for his handling as a chauffeur since for how fast he was going and for the roads he drives he did very well, the problem is that we seemed won in the back, especially me who was in the last seat. It was impossible to sleep or relax as I was jumping all the time. Now I claim because I had no heating!!! We suffered from the cold on the last day Saturday 12th back to the border from Villa Mar. It was minus 3 degrees and despite how warm we were we froze on top of that jeep. Besides Luis has a bad speedometer, I never saw how fast he was driving. Now I have a claim for the services provided, the food was dropping in quality as the days went by. On day 3 in Villa Mar we weren't even given dessert, sir said it was only for day 1. On day 4 we had breakfast in the polquen baths, poor breakfast a hard and very cold bread and only gave us egg. According to Luis, he said it was what the agency gave him. We saw other groups had fruits, yogurt, milk, cereal, hot cake, dulce de leche etc. And we just egg, it was super unworthy. As for the accommodations we pay extra for room and private bathroom. The bathroom in villa sea was horrible when opening the door you had to go first to the shower, close the door and occupy the toilet! I didn't have a curtain. The shower I imagine is for you to go through the shower first. But the whole bathroom got wet, literally flooded. Bone wasn't worth paying extras for!

review_text: The museum is on top of Cerro Artlleria but, unfortunately, the Artilleria ascensor is broken. There is a collectivo that goes to the top but the cabs were all full when they went by us on the bottom of the hill. We walked to Plaza Echaurren to find a taxi. The museum is on the small side but aided greatly by English signs for almost every exhibit. Here you learn about the military men who have streets named after them in Valpo and the battles that shaped the country. The last room is dedicated to the founder of the museum whom my husband remembered as one of the coup leaders described in the human rights museum in Santiago. I guess museum founding trumps human rights. There is a reduced entrance fee for seniors. Next to the museum, at the top of the hill, are a variety of handicraft stalls. I saw a greater selection of shawls here than anywhere else in Valpo or Vina. It's a relatively easy (Hey! This is Valparaiso!) walk back down.

review_text: The Church of San Francisco the oldest church on the archipelago , located on one side of the Plaza de Armas in Castro, is oldest church on the archipelago and is now declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 30 November 2000. It as built to replace an earlier church that was burned down. The exterior is bright yellow and purple and is constructed of galvanized iron. The interior is awash with warm, varnished wood. The woodwork throughout the church is stunning with its use of native woods such as larch, cypress, and a Chilean evergreen tree. The church has rows of stained-glass windows. Built by local Castro carpenters, wooden dowels were used instead of nails for the joints. Reinforced wooden joints hold the building in place. The wood construction is believed to provide insulation against the cold. Back in the early 17th century and onward to the 19th century, the Jesuits and Franscicans missionaries “circular mission”, resulted in the construction of 70 churches. They were built on high ground to serve as a navigation beacon and to protect them from rain and flooding. Of the 70 churches, only 16 remain. Some were destroyed by earthquake, fire, or tidal waves. It is well worth your time to visit this church ore one of the 15 others located on Chiole Island. Some you won’t be able to miss – look for the bright colored ones.

review_text: We hiked from the park at the bottom of the mountain, all the way to the Statue at the top. The beautiful vistas along the way only slightly prepared us for the incredible view at the top. Standing at the base of the statue you take in all of Santiago in all directions. Best of all, though was the peace of the place. This, like most high vistas that have statues at the top, was loaded with visitors. However, even given the number of people there, it was quiet and felt like a religious shrine should feel, quiet, peaceful, and reflective. You can't drive the entire way to the top. But, even though it is quite a distance, if this 74 year old can do it, almost anyone should be able, and believe me when I say that if you are visiting Santiago, this is a place not to be missed.

review_text: We went to Casa Vina for a tasting, tour and also lunch. I booked ahead via email and had prompt and helpful response. We arrived for 1pm lunch in the restaurant which was such a beautiful outdoor patio. Our menu was really good and included great wine, although would book to do the a la cart menu instead of the set menu if we were going back. Our server was great and helped us get back to the other side of the vineyard for our tasting after lunch. The tour of the property was really enjoyable. We got to see rooms in the hotel, the old car collection along with all the wine cellars. I usually fine wine tours a bit boring but this was simply great! After our tour and tasting we were allowed to take their bikes to explore the property more, then we bought another bottle of wine and sat outside enjoying the sun. I highly recommend going to this place with extra time to really enjoy it. Transport - we did not want to do a typical wine tour, but also did not want anyone to have to drive and miss out in wines. On the way to Casa Silva we took the bus from Santiago to San Fernando and then took a quick Uber to the vineyard. We were headed to Santa Cruz from there and the wonderful attendant at the gate helped us get a local bus back down to the bus station where it was easy to get a big bus to Santa Cruz.

review_text: We contacted Zerando Chile to hire the transfer service for tours in Santiago and on the snow, in private mode, since we were in a group of 8 people, including a 5-year-old child. The choice of private transfer was made to have flexibility in arrival and departure times. The initial service was quick and efficient, with the Reservation being made without difficulty. However, the experience during the tours was disappointing. - **Day 1 (Laguna del Inca):** The driver demonstrated imprudence when driving at high speed in the curves, using the cell phone at the wheel. - **Day 2 (Farellones):** During the journey, we were stopped at an inspection, and to our surprise, the van was with the documentation late. We stopped on the road, in an isolated location, for about 1h30 until another van arrived. This made us miss all morning in the park, causing a significant disorder as it was also the birthday of one of the members of the group. Upon arrival at the park, the driver suggested that we stay until the closure of the site (17h) due to the delay, but we need to leave a little earlier (16h30) due to an emergency with the child, and the driver was not there in the matched place, we had to wait with the child all wet and quite cold (he arrived after 17h). - **Day 3 (City tour):** The experience was good, with emphasis on the explanations of the Guide Cintia. - **Day 4 (Ski Day in El Colorado):** The driver (other) also wanted to match a return time. I warned that we would see the time we wanted to leave and would warn by message. When I warned that we were ready, we took a while and went to the parking lot and again had to wait for your arrival. - **Day 5 (Winery Undurraga):** The shared transfer was timely and took place without any problems. The transfer requested privately to ensure greater comfort ended up not meeting our expectations. The problem was not the agreed time, but rather that we chose a private van to have more convenience, such as being able to decide to leave sooner or later, or pick up something in the van if necessary. However, as the drivers were not available at the time we needed, this became impossible. In short, what should have been a quiet experience turned into a great stress. We requested a discount or the rental of clothes for the next tour as compensation for what happened in Farellones, which was accepted by the agency. However, this does not erase the numerous inconveniences we have encountered that have not been mentioned here either. Lamentamos profundamente que sua experiência conosco tenha sido negativa, e agradecemos imensamente seu feedback. Anuncio que mediante os feedbacks negativos, implantamos uma reestruturação completa no nosso setor logístico e de transfers para o ano de 2025. Sabemos que isso não recupera sua experiência negativa, mas valorizamos imensamente seu detalhamento nas situações ocorridas e esperamos que tenham experiências positivas no destino no futuro.

review_text: We booked our tour with the only company that provides them, VTS. We specifically booked an English tour. Once we were underway (bus had left the pickup point) we were told there would be no English spoken, and there was no English written description provided either. There were a total of 8 "English speaking only" people on this tour (out of perhaps a total of 30 people) who had all been told to come on this specific date and time as it would be conducted in English. When we tried to speak to the tour guide about this (with the assistance of someone who could translate) all he would say is "it is not my fault that I don't speak English". When we sent an email to the company after the tour to express our concern about the situation and to request a partial refund we got no response. Very poor customer service overall. The town is very interesting to see but now that a tour of the mine itself is no longer allowed the tour does not warrant a full day. Even the people who understood Spanish seemed to be milling about waiting for the tour to "move along". The stop at the little town on the way back to the pickup spot seemed to be totally pointless and a "filler". Overall, an interesting visit to a ghost mining town that warrants a partial day tour.

review_text: Amazing walk with beautiful views during the rise and the possibility of staying on the edge of the crater at the end of the rise, a unique experience. But don’t be fooled by the distance: there are only 3km of climb, but at more than 5000m altitude any meter makes the difference. Are 600m of elevation gain, that's enough at this altitude. The agencies sell the ride as a medium difficulty, but it is NOT. Me and my husband are experienced trekkers and we have already made hiking in altitude, and every walk in this environment is difficult. Acclimation in other places of San Pedro, such as geysers, the highland lagoons, will help us not to feel the pain of altitude, such as headache, nausea, dizziness, but will not improve the lack of air, which is the big problem of this type of trekking. There is much less oxygen at this altitude and we feel very tired and lack of breath. You walk much slower than usual. It takes us about 3:30 to get to the crater. If you have done other walks in altitude and know how your body reacts to this condition, you can go without a guide (we went alone), because the track is super marked and there is no way to go wrong. If you have never walked in altitude or have no trekking experience, then the presence of a guide, who can assist with extra oxygen, if necessary, is essential. In any case, I suggest climbing Cerro Toco first, which is a shorter and less steep walk, to see if the body is well adapted to altitude.

review_text: SNOW IN CHILE: for those who do not want to ski and want to see only snow, it is worth the panoramic tour that the agencies sell. In it you spend almost the whole day walking through the snow without having to enter the stations. The Farellones park is cool, but the perrengue of the queues is not worth a little, I think. Farellones seems to be more fun for kids. This tour may be exhausting, but still worth it. The restaurant they stop at Farellones is not good and is quite expensive. Take your snack for the whole day. CLOTHING: what is really needed is cold protection. Up there the cold is freezing. I recommend: thermal half and second half, thermal trousers underneath, thermal t-shirt underneath, a blouse and jacket on top, hat or ear protector and snow gloves. Regarding the snow, if you are not skiing and you are not snowing on the day of the tour, a timberland style booth is already enough. If you need, just rent the boots. With tennis I find it complicated because it slips and wet. If snow is falling, it is important that your clothes are at least rain resistant. If you're going to ski you need the full kit. I saw a lot of people renting the full kit without having to. And worse, I haven't seen any guidance on this. Review of: Panoramic Farellones tour does not include entrance to the park / optional on your own

review_text: We went up by bus and walked down. The bus ride up was very scenic. It took about 15 minutes. It felt sketchy so we went back up the trail and took the paved road down the mountain. It took us two and a half hours but it was a very scenic route where we took amazing photos of the tallest building in South America.

review_text: The tour is very expensive which cost 80,000 peso and yet didn't deliever up to our expectation. Make sure you're physically fit enough to do the continuous 5 hrs trekking uphill continuously. We asked a few agencies prior trekking, none informed that the possibility of lift closing due to wind & cancellation procedure details given only if you ask. We followed a tour from Norte Sur agency, after we pay the full sum of money, we need to try our clothes and equipment. They don't have my exact shoes size. Besides, When we ask about if cancellation due to weather, as long as they reach camp base then there's a charge which is not refundable. Fine. When we arrive at the morning, it's windy, first thing they said, today no lift, it's your decision whether to going up or not. Hello, then why am i paying money to here. I walked slower compare to the rest, they keep saying I'm not gonna to make it with my pace and the last part is way to steep for me. I tried to communicate with them a few times like i try to walk faster to decide later whether to go for the final path; i walk whatever i can even doesn't get to the top and whether i can reach the top 30mins later. But they dont seem to get me as i find they have limited english. Fine. They only matter whether you can reach the top by 1pm so they can come down not too late. Thus, I didn't do the last path but if given me more time i know that i can complete it. The things that really make me disatisfy about the tour is 1) I'm not paying this money for you to discourage me to reach the top; 2) if you're only keen to brought up fit ppl to the top at your time then why not you warn us upfront before we even decided to go this tour so that you only bring good hikers; 3) we didn't even get to experience the snow sliding down but walked the ice back instead; 4) why can't you just break into a smaller group for slow hikers to bring us to the top. There are 4 persons out of 11 didn't make it to the top, in fact my feet wasn't that tired compare to my Cerro Castillo hiking which was much painful but yet i completed within estimated time as per map.

review_text: We went looking to buy a bunch of different wines for a tasting we were doing later with a large group. Javier and Christopher pulled out an amazing selection of wines for us to try (for a totally reasonable fee given we opened 16 bottles), telling us not just about the wines, but also the vineyards and winemakers! Working with about 55 small producers has meant they have a unique selection of great wines with greater stories, and they were happy to share them all! The relationships they have with their winemakers are special-- Christopher talked about how he and Anahí (the co-owner & Christopher's wife, who we didn't get to meet) only work with producers they would share a barbecue with (and who make great wine). Friendly & knowledgeable people, a beautiful space, affordable prices, and wonderful wines-- we could not have asked for a better place! If you are at all interested in exploring Chilean wines from some smaller names (and some famous small producers), La Cava del Barrio is a must-visit!

review_text: You know those iconic photos of Santiago nestled in the foot of the Andes that you find when you do a Google search on the city? Well, they were probably taken from Cerro San Cristobal. The hill is dotted with manicured lawns, pretty gardens, a zoo and swimming pools (very pricey admission for the pools), and is a great place to spend those hot summer days at. It is particularly crowded on weekends so try to visit on a weekday. The furnicular is now opened (it was shut for renovations when we were there) so you can the choice of taking a 2-hour hike or a quick and convenient furnicular ride (from the Bellavista entrance) up the hill. There are two entrances you can access the hill from - Bellavista (15 minutes walk from Metro Baquedano) and Providencia (20 minutes walk from Metro Valdivia).

review_text: I´ve been living in Santiago for over four years and the capitol is often seen as a transient town for travellers heading up north to the desert and beaches and down south to the lakes region and Torres del Paine. However being here for so many years I have come to appreciate how much it has actually changed from the old grey place where there was nothing to do or see into a city with many attractions. Complete barrios are being renovated, cultural centres and museums are popping up everywhere and there are a variety of activities. Foto Ruta seems to have picked up on this movement. I first heard of it when I was in Buenos Aires and thought I’d give it a try here in my home town. A small group met up on a sunny afternoon in a small café in the Barrio Lastarria. After about 45 minutes of introduction, some tips and inspirational photos we were handed a list of clues, a map of the area and off we were. I am a keen photographer, but funnily enough I had never taken many pictures in Santiago. After about 2 hours we spent wandering around the beautiful streets and taking our photos I came back with a bunch I was quite proud of and found it quite hard to choose my favourites. The event ended over a glass of wine with everybody in the group discussing their photos and comments and a short analysis from the host of the event, Cat Allen, a professional photographer located in Santiago. Summing up I would say Foto Ruta is a great way to spend an afternoon in Santiago, getting to know the historical parts of town and improving your photographic skills.

review_text: Riding the Carretera Austal of Chile’s Patagonia region was a bucket list item for several of those in our riding group. We could not have picked better guides and partners for this adventure than Moto Patagonia and its owner/operators, Daniel and Paula. The experience was both challenging and highly rewarding. Daniel and Paula run a top-shelf operation. The bikes are late model, extraordinarily clean, and very well maintained (Daniel is an accomplished mechanic). The level of customized, personal service they provide is second-to-none. They are professionals and just good people. Daniel and Paula helped us navigate the multiple hurdles to entering Chile during the COVID pandemic. Without their help, we probably would not have successfully made this trip. Hopefully, the bureaucratic process will ease as time goes on. The environs and scenery of Southern Chile are nothing less than breathtaking. Many of us have ridden extensively in the Western US and Europe. What you see and experience in Patagonia is like no other region that I have seen: unique and awe-inspiring, kilometer after kilometer. You will want to stop more frequently for photos than the schedule allows, at times. Daniel knows the region, culture, language, restaurants, and lodges (and their owners) intimately. He runs these trips like we are family (which you become by the end of the ride). The riding is challenging. At times, there is a pretty high pucker factor, unless you have been riding dirt since childhood and this is second nature to you. It was certainly more challenging than any of us expected, given that we are all mostly street riders. It is rated as a 4/5 in difficulty for a reason. Be prepared for that. Daniel necessarily runs a tight ship to keep the group on schedule when needed. That is what a good leader and guide does. Nevertheless, there are some long days on the saddle. And, riding stretches in the rain — highly likely at some point along the way — can be hair-raising and challenging, both physically and mentally. I would not recommend this for casual riders who not in relatively good physical shape. All in all, Moto Patagonia deserves a 5-star rating. The personal attention, experiential customization, excellent equipment and bikes, and Daniel’s expert guidance on the road makes this a not-to-miss adventure for those looking to ride on the wild side of the Southern Hemisphere. Thank you so much, we certainly had some Covid hurdles to get through but it was worth it once we got on the road riding! I'm glad you enjoyed riding with us so much. Great Experience for everyone.

review_text: From the first day we started looking into Patagonia trips, we were in touch with Carrie at Venture Patagonia. She was very attentive and gave us advice on when best to come for the W trek and what to do in Puerto Natales afterwards. We had a wonderful bespoke package where all food was included, all accommodation was sorted and all extras were organised in advance. When we arrived, our local buses were late (which is apparently very common!) but we made it to the guest house to be very warmly greeted with tea, home made Chilean cookies and a wonderful dinner. We had a thourough introduction to our trek and shown to our lovely nearby hotel as the guest house was full and they helped with our bags. Bright and early in the morning we were taken to the start of the trek, the driver kindly stopped en route showing us the wildlife like guanacos, foxes and nandus so we could take pictures. The W trek was fantastic, Patagonia is honestly the most beautiful place on earth, we had a guide for the first day up to the base of the towers, and on our last couple of days so that Eason, from the company, could take some promo pics and videos. Every refugio was great and food was all included so we didn't need to carry any sleeping bags/food/cooking equipment which was very nice! Luckily Carrie advised us to come at the shoulder season so a large portion of the trek we were by ourselves and only occasionally over took people or let people overtake us but mostly it was us and nature. I hear this is completely different in high season, where there are back to back queues nearly round the whole trail, so I definitely recommend going in October or other quieter times, if you can. Don't let it put you off though, this is definitely one of the world's best treks! We went kayaking on the grey lake infront of the glacier, walked up to the hanging bridges, reached all the fantastic view points, saw the torres del paine towers and so much wildlife! We also expirienced all the strong Patagonian wind, snow, rain, beating sun and cold every day, it was so varied. Patagonia weather is crazy but we loved it. We went to a local spa for a massage the day after we finished which was recommended by Venture Patagonia and extremely good and well deserved. Next we went on a wine tasting experience which was superb, it was just us and so nice to taste and purchase delicious chilean wine! The following day we did the estancia day. It was a day on a ranch, reached by boat up a fjord, where we had freshly open fire-cooked lamb for lunch, went on horse rides, watched the estancia dogs and a sheep sheering demonstration. It was a brilliant day out and i'm so pleased we did it. Carrie also kindly took us to a local handcraft shop so we could buy some things made from the estancia wool and made locally. The only downside of the whole trip was that our ice trekking trip was sadly cancelled on the day due to a carving of the glacier, but we flawlessly got our money back from Big Foot via Venture Patagonia. To summarise, this was without a doubt one of the best trips we've ever been on. We were extremely well looked after from start to finish and the whole trip was incredibly well organised. Hello from the whole team here at Venture Patagonia! Thank you for your kind review-we are happy that you enjoyed so much of what Patagonia has to offer. We look forward to welcoming you back to Puerto Natales and hopefully you can give the ice trekking another go. Best of luck in your next adventure! Best regards, Carrie

review_text: We went on an organized tour, which is important for the permits needed to pass through security. The facility is only open to the public either one day a week or one day a month, and the drive is long and arduous if not a local. The professional guide resident at the observatory itself was a practicing astronomer and exceptionally knowledgeable. We were provided supervised access to both of the main observatories and these were truly awesome in dimension and import. We only wish we had been there at night, to see the clear skies on the mountain top. This was a once in a lifetime opportunity and was a highlight of our South American trip. The drive is on a dirt road and it is necessary to pass a gated check point, permit required. The road then is long and passes along 2-3 valleys with scrub land with gradual assent until the final climb to the mountain top. When the observatories are first spotted, they seem remote and high. To avoid light pollution, to have dry air, and little dust in this arid locale, the peak is an ideal spot; the entire area is set aside for this purpose, a real commitment of the government to astronomical research. The telescopes and cameras are of course state of the art. The physical dimensions of them and of the observatory structures are amazing. Glad to have had this opportunity. Did I say, "Awesome!!"?

review_text: Very well organised thanks to Eric's attention to detail and great staff. We wanted for nothing. Our guide Nelcon had a seemingly inexhaustible supply of information, a good command of English, and a passion for the Bolivian Andes, its flora and fauna. It's a fascinating trip and there is a lot to see. The joy of Bolivia is that it largely remains in its natural state and everything we saw was well worth the rough roads to get there. It would be lunacy to attempt this without a very good 4x4 and an experienced guide. The roads reach around 5000m altitude and it is cold but it's a trip of a lifetime and a privilege to have done it. We stayed in the Jardines de Mallcu, the only hotel with heating in tiny, remote Villamar which was money well spent. And the Jardines de Uyuni which was super and good value. A family of 4 with driver and guide with luggage on top and daysacks in the cabin was about right for a 7 seater Land Cruiser. Hot and tasty lunches were much appreciated.

review_text: While we were in Valaraiso for three days, we had a guide named Juan Victor Reyes through this company, for three days. The first day Juan took us on a walking tour through the city. We took the local bus service, took the Funicular down from the top of the city, as well as took the underground tunnel to an underground elevator that took us to the bottom of the city. We saw all the major highlights of the city, and went to areas where we would not have gone had we done this ourselves. Juan took us to a nice little restaurant for lunch. The second day Juan took us in a van with a driver to Vina del Mar and up the coast line to see the sites. We stopped at a fishing village and obseverved a large number of penguins. At the end of the day we stopped at the area where the ships dock and observed sea lions. On the third day we had a young man name Jaime who works for Juan, with the same driver, and he took us to four vineyards, two of them we had wine tastings. When that was complete he took us to our hotel in Santiago. These two young men were very professional, knowledgable, friendly and courteous. I would definately refer this tour company to anyone. Well worth the money. The scenery was amazing..........

review_text: Perched 860ms above sea level in Metropolitan Park and overlooking the city on both sides, San Cristobal is one of the must see attractions when in Santiago. This magnificent statue of Christ, towers over the Santuario de la Inmaculada Concepcion, and is a very popular place of pilgrimage with the local residents particularly on the weekend. The little church, the sanctuary, the garden of contemplation and special cemeteries are pleasantly laid out so that visitors are aware of their religious significance and are respectful when there. However, this area is a tourist trap with its cafes, shops and excellent 360 degree vantage points overlooking the city and gets very crowded. Top tip. Take the Teleferico ( Metropolitan Park side ) up and the funicular down ( Bellavista neighbourhood ). Not open on Mondays. If you are on the hop on hop off bus the rides up and down are included in the price.

review_text: Wow, I guess we really missed the point of this place –I was looking forward to it and we arrived by car from Vina del Mar - after going through the country road cut thru from Limache - so, along the coast north of Valpo and got caught up in the one way streets, big crowds of people, graffiti, grime, rundown buildings in the area just off the port. We tried to drive up to the hills to get a glimpse of the character of the place we heard about (UNESO Heritage site!) but, ran into a dead-end run-down dirt road with crumbling buildings, mangy dogs, trash and … need I go on? We heard, afterwards, that you really need to know where to go to see the better part of Valpo (historic, colorful funky, buildings – a small area). It’s a working port and a busy city (not just for tourists) and we were prepared for that, but not for the run down and confusing streets. Next time we’ll have to try to approach this city from the big Santiago highway 68 coming from the east … and give it another try. We ended up going up the coast to a small beachside town and enjoyed that part of the Chilean coast instead.

review_text: Anyone traveling to Santiago do NOT use MTO Tours!! They falsely advertise themselves. They can be found through Tripadvisor and Viator as well as they have a Facebook page. We thought we did our research before booking the Small Group Pre-Post Cruise Vina del Mar, Valparaiso and Casablanca Wine Tour with 8 or less people, in which they had good reviews at the time of booking but it was the WORST tour we have ever been on!!! They sent us a confirmation email, like every other tour we have booked. However, they had no directions such as time, meeting place, who to look for, etc. So both my mom & I reached out to them for clarification through email and WhatsApp.We only got a response through Whatsapp, that they would contact us first thing in the morning. When we hadn’t heard from them by 8am we reached out to them again through Whatsapp. The response we got was “Driver is in port, No More Calls”. We waited an hour with several other people who booked different excursions with MTO at the Port of San Antonio before one person wandered a few blocks away and found the tour bus. If anyone has gone through the port of San Antonio, the neighborhood surrounding it is pretty sketchy for foreigners. Finally, the guide followed her back to the port with a sign that had several parties listed on it that totalled 32 individuals. They had combined several small groups into one large tour group and gave us an option of going with them or staying at the port, with no refund or other alternatives being offered. Because of having 32 people on the tour, our luggage had to follow us in a separate vehicle. We waited over an hour on the bus before they started the “tour”. Our guide immediately blamed us for starting late, which was not even remotely the case. It was clearly MTO’s fault because of very poor communication prior to the start of the tour. He said because some of our group was late that they would have to skip part of the tour. Once we started the tour, our guide off-handedly explained that they are not set up for tours like this, that they typically only provide transportation for people to the cruise ports, hotels & airport. This tour was something new whey started a couple of weeks prior and it had not been going well, but to please leave a good review so the company can keep trying to make it better. They were really vague about what locations we were stopping by or what we would be doing along the way. By the time we got to the first stop, which was a view from the top of the hill in Valparaiso, most of us had been on the bus for over 4 hours. At this point several people started to inquire about bathrooms. The guide told us there were no restrooms in the area set up to accommodate 32 of us and there was nothing he could do. After push back from pretty much everyone, he was able to locate a restroom for us. From there we stopped at Vina Del Mar to see the garden clock for 10 minutes, then we were bused to lunch where they gave us 2 hours. This seemed like too much time considering what the tour was really offering, but in hindsight, we were glad we had a chance to eat. Shortly after we left the lunch spot, the guide told us the van carrying our luggage had broken down. He made it sound like another van would be right there to pick up our luggage and catch up with us at the next stop. By the time we got to the winery in Casablanca (which is what our party had signed up for) we were only given 30 minutes for a tour & tasting, which is clearly not enough time. Two of our party paid for a tasting they were unable to do because our guide rushed us back on the bus. We were then told the plan was to tour Santiago, drop off the parties who had hotels, then go to the airport to drop off the passengers flying out that evening. That’s when we discovered that our luggage was far from us. The guide kept saying it was only 45 minutes out and that he was in contact with the driver, but then the story changed. He didn’t know who the driver was and only had information about him through his manager. He said we just needed to move on and our luggage would arrive at our hotels later (not sure how that would be the case as none of our luggage was marked for which hotel). One of the parties said they were going to be far too late to the airport if they stayed on for the tour and asked that they be dropped off at the airport first. The guide said they would, but that would mean the rest of us would not be able to have the tour of Santiago. Everyone on the bus agreed to this plan, no problem. But then the guide said they would leave them at the airport and the luggage would have to catch up to them later. Because they would have to wait for their luggage, they could not go through security and would have to wait. At this point no one on the bus had any trust in the guide and no one was getting calls or messages through to the MTO manager, they were just being hung up on. By the time we got to the airport, we collectively refused to leave the bus or airport without our luggage, but our guide said it was not his problem and he and the driver needed to get home for dinner with their families. Absolutely UNACCEPTABLE! The guide played a message from his manager, supposedly, who was just saying to trust them and they would get us our luggage. Trust wasn’t going to happen after a whole day of lies from them and lack of compassion or respect for any of us! A couple of us had trackers in our luggage and were able to get a better ETA of our bags and they were nearly 2 hours out! And this after we had been led on with 45 minute promises for several hours! The guide continued to be a complete jerk and told us we have to move on, that they needed to start their weekend. If we wanted to wait for our luggage we could stay at the airport or if we refused to get off the bus then we could spend the night on the bus. One of the ladies in another party went into the airport and came back with security. While they weren’t able to do anything directly, their presence stopped the guide from arguing with us about waiting for the luggage or getting us to our hotels once it showed up. After 3 hours of sitting at the airport on the bus, our luggage finally arrived. It was the only way all of us would have gotten our luggage back. We were finally able to check into our hotel around 11:30 PM, after being on the bus from 9am - 14½ hours for a tour that was supposed to be a small group and last only 7-8 hours! There were a few others still on the bus needing to be dropped off at their hotel after we were dropped off. We later learned that the driver & guide started drinking beers and didn’t get the last person to their hotel, which was only a couple blocks from ours, until 12:30 AM. This company shouldn’t be in business nor should this guide be allowed to give tours. Review of: Small Group Pre-Post Cruise Viña del Mar Valparaiso and Casablanca Winery tour Thank you for sharing your experience with us! Our mission is to provide the best quality tours for our customers, so we are always apologetic when unfortunate things like these happen. We'll work hard to be better in the future. MTO Tour Team

review_text: The architecture and design of this museum is world-class, and a visit is essential in attempting to understand Chilean history during the Pinochet years—and Chile’s own attempts to come to grips with it. For English speakers with weak to nonexistent Spanish the English audio guide is a must. After you enter up the ramp, you are in a voluminous main hall, but the narrative is carried by two long narrow galleries on the sides, on this floor and the one above. The numbers for the audio guide are pretty much in sequence, so look for them—the numbers can be a bit hidden among the pictures and Spanish prose— and try to follow the sequence. To get the full narrative, allow at least two hours, probably more. But even a briefer visit can be rewarding, simply for the architecture and the spirit of the museum.

review_text: A Night Sky tour is a must in San Pedro de Atacama - don't leave this region without doing one of these remarkable tours. The Atacama Desert is one of the best places in the world to star gaze - high altitude and a dry climate in a remote location with very little light pollution. I did a Night Sky tour with Space Orbs (aka San Pedro de Atacama Celestial Exploration) office located at Caracoles 166 and it was amazing! We were picked up in town by large buses, splitting the group into Spanish and English speaking, and driven out into the Atacama Desert (about 30 min drive) to the observation area. The tour was approximately 2 hours, the first hour was an informative introduction to the night sky of the southern hemisphere, given outside identifying different stars and planets. The second hour was dedicated to looking through the many telescopes on site (must be at least 15) all different types and sizes - that are set to view specific parts of the sky (outlined by the guides). You are then given time to view the sky through each of these telescopes. It was an incredible experience - one I will never forget! Loved it!

review_text: My husband and I spent three days and two nights in San Pedro de Atacama. Starting with the planning of the trip to its conclusion, our experience with Pablo was exemplary. Before we booked with him, he patiently explained (he speaks Spanish, English, and French) what might be worth seeing in the time we had and customized the itinerary to fit our preferences. He didn’t do any sales pitch, or try to sell us additional packages. His outfit is no frills or luxury, but a comfortable, customized, and unique experience. A few distinguishing things about Pablo: Pablo knows and loves the Atacama Desert which shows in his great knowledge and understanding of the area, from naming each type of rock, shrub, bird, and animal as well as all the interesting sites. Pablo also took us to some lesser-known areas that were not visited by too many tourists. He respects nature and humans’ impact on nature which is important to us as well. He also knows a great deal about astronomy including naming and showing in the sky the location of more stars, planets, nebulas, and constellations than we ever knew about. He also would give us great geology lessons along the way by explaining various geological aspects that helped shaped the area. He was thoughtful enough and brought us a bottle of wine and cheese to have at the end of our first day in the middle of the desert while we enjoyed a magical sunset with no one around. Pablo also picked us up and dropped us off at the Calama airport, and even waited for us at the airport to make sure we were checked in before he left. If you want to intimately experience the real Atacama Desert without a throng of people in big vans with a friendly and highly knowledgeable person, we highly recommend Pablo. Muchas gracias, Pablo! We hope to come back again!

review_text: If you have to choose only one winery to go in colchagua valley, go to this one... Here they follow the "intervene the less you can" lemma in wine production to the extreme. No pumps, no filters, no machines,... everything is handled manually and the winery is built vertically so that the wine can follow to the next one through gravity. The architecture of the winery is astonishing...the winery was built in the rock and on the top, you can have one of the greatest views of colchagua valley, if not the greatest...

review_text: We spent two nights at the wonderful lodge with our great bird guide Rafa Di Biase from Birds Chile. This private property is around 40,000 acres. The owner Patricio Campos bought the property in the 1980's and has spent considerable time and effort on developing trails and roads. He has a really nice lodge where we had a great room and first class meals This park is truly wild forest that Patricio is preserving at his own expense. The problem is that the bridge has washed out that gave land access to the park and you have to take a 20 minute ride in a boat across the lake to get to the lodge. It really is not a big problem and is part of the adventure. You have the opportunity to see several rare endemic species in this park. We saw the tiny Pudu deer on the lawn in front of the lodge. There was sign of the rare Darwin Fox but we did not see one. Also, the extremely rare Kod Kod cat can be found here. There are lots of birds and the trails in the forest are well maintained and just beautiful. We would have been happy to stay an extra day. We felt sorry for Patricio that this lodge is not more visited because of the access. It is well worth the time to go down there if you want to see really wild original Chiloe forest. The lodge is really nice and we had great service and food. You just need to call ahead to have him meet you with a boat to take you to the lodge. We had the all inclusive rooms. They also have 2 cabins where you can stay with a family.

review_text: Okay, you will need to awake too early in the morning (not exactly in the morning, I mean) as El Tatio is far from San Pedro de Atacama's touristic city - and the roads are too bad (why not? you are in the very heart of the most arid desert in the world - Atacama's Desert). After more than 1 hour, before sunrise, you will be entering in El Tatio, and the temperature will be much less than zero Celsius degrees. So, be prepared, and take with you layers and layers of warm clothes, as I did. Geysers are impressive. You will walk close to them, fading yourself in the mist, hearing the water boiling below the ground and freezing. The experience is completed with a bath in Pozo Rustico, a kind of naturally heated pool. Sometimes the sand in the ground of the pool will burn your feet, but don't worry: taking a bath seeing the geysers and the volcanos surrounding you, the sun shining in the deeply blue sky, is priceless.

review_text: The place is perfect to enjoy the marvelous properties of the hot spring waters and it is around 40 min. from Pucon by a paved road. We went on a rainy day and we have a great time. The "Termas" had available 4 small indoors pools with a calm and inviting ambient, with chairs around the pools.They had 1 covered outdoor pool and 1 outdoor, you have lounges and chairs where to seat listening the sound of the current of a small river and looking the mountains. The pools temperature were 80F. I got a bath in the cold river which I found so invigorating even with the rain. But you could get the cold showers too.BTW I suggest to bring water shoes for entering the river due the river rocks. I strongly advice you to don't miss the trail and stroll a little bit , you won't regret it. They have an spa too, for those who want to de-stress completely. My son was really happy with his deep tissue massage. The facilities and pools were very clean. The restaurant is good with a decent menu and food is good.People who work there were really friendly. Muchas gracias por su comentario. Esperamos que nos vuelva a visitar.
